paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The British grass interrupted brome was once declared extinct, like the dodo. Named for its gappy seed head, this unprepossessing grass was found nowhere else in the world. Victorian-era gardening experts were the first to record it. In the early 20th century, it grew widely across southern England, but it quickly vanished and by 1972 could no longer be found. Even seeds stored at Cambridge University Botanic Garden as an insurance policy were dead because they had mistakenly been kept at room temperature. Admirers of the grass were devastated.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Reports of its disappearance, however, were not entirely correct. Interrupted brome has enjoyed a revival that owes little to science. Thanks to one gardening enthusiast, it now thrives as a pot plant. The prospect of reintroducing Britain’s almost-extinct grass into the wild has excited conservationists everywhere.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: At first, Philip Smith did not realise that this highly unusual grass was growing at his home. When he heard that it had become extinct, he decided to surprise his fellow botanists. At a meeting of the British Botanical Society in Manchester in 1979, he seized his opportunity. After lamenting the demise of interrupted brome and saying, ‘What a pity we did not study it further!’, he suddenly displayed his pots of the supposedly ‘extinct’ grass for everyone to see.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Smith had preserved seeds collected in 1963 from the grass’s last stronghold at Pampisford, just as it began to disappear from the wild. He cultivated the grass year after year. Ultimately, his curiosity about the plant—not a scientific or technological project—saved it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For now, the future of interrupted brome is secure. Seeds from Smith’s plants have been safely stored in the cutting-edge facilities of the Millennium Seed Bank at Wakehurst Place in Sussex, while living plants thrive in the botanic gardens at Kew, Edinburgh and Cambridge. Seeds have also been saved at sites across the country, and the grass now flourishes in several public gardens.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The grass will now be reintroduced to the British countryside. As part of the Species Recovery Project, English Nature plans to return interrupted brome to the agricultural landscape, provided willing farmers can be found. Unfortunately, the grass is neither beautiful nor practical; it is unquestionably a weed that few people value today. It was probably never widespread enough to trouble farmers, and no one now prizes its productivity or nutritional qualities. As a crop, it leaves much to be desired by agriculturalists.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Smith’s research has sought to discover where the grass came from and points to mutations in other weedy grasses as the most likely source. Its relationship to soft brome is so close that the great Victorian taxonomist Professor Hackel initially classified interrupted brome as merely a variety of that species. George Claridge Druce, a nineteenth-century botanist, recorded the grass and convinced his peers that it deserved recognition as a species in its own right. Despite growing up in poverty and being self-taught, Druce became the leading botanist of his time.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The origin of the grass may be clear, but the timing of its emergence is harder to determine. One clue lies in its tendency to grow as a weed in fields containing fodder crops, particularly nitrogen-fixing legumes such as sainfoin, lucerne and clover. According to agricultural historian Joan Thirsk, humble sainfoin and its companions were first recorded in Britain in the early 17th century. Seeds imported from the Continent were sown in pastures to feed horses and other livestock. At first, however, only a few enthusiastic gentlemen used the new crops for their prized horses.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: Before long, the need to feed parliamentary armies in Scotland, England and Ireland became more pressing than ever, and farmers had to produce more bread, cheese and beer. By 1650, legumes were increasingly incorporated into arable rotations as green manure to boost grain yields. Nathaniel Fiennes’s Sainfoin Improved, a bestseller published in 1671, helped spread the word. With the arrival of sainfoin, clover and lucerne, Britain’s own rogue grass had suddenly appeared.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text: Although credit for discovering interrupted brome belongs to Miss A. M. Barnard, who collected the first specimens at Odsey, Bedfordshire, in 1849, the grass had probably lurked undetected in the English countryside for at least a century. Smith believes that this botanical equivalent of the dodo probably evolved in the late 17th or early 18th century, once sainfoin became established. The rise of the motor car and the consequent decline in fodder crops for horses caused the brome’s fortunes to fall rapidly during the 20th century. Sainfoin has now almost vanished from the countryside, although its colourful flowers occasionally appear in lowland nature reserves. More recently, artificial fertilisers have made legume rotations unnecessary.

paragraphs.label: K
paragraphs.text: This close association with unfashionable crops creates problems for anyone seeking to re-establish interrupted brome in the modern countryside. Like many once-common arable weeds, including corncockle, its seeds do not survive long in the soil. Each spring, the brome depended on farmers resowing its seeds; before weedkillers and sophisticated seed sieves, plentiful brome seed would have contaminated stocks of crop seed. Fragile seeds are not its only problem: the species is also reluctant to release them as they ripen. According to Smith, the grass will struggle even under optimal conditions and cannot easily compete with the more resilient plants of today’s improved agricultural landscape.

paragraphs.label: L
paragraphs.text: Nevertheless, interrupted brome’s inability to thrive independently may offer some benefits. Any farmer willing to foster this unique part of the world’s flora can be confident that it will never become an invasive pest. Restoring the grass to its rightful home could bring further benefits, particularly if this unusual species is recognised as a national treasure. British farmers gave interrupted brome the opportunity to evolve in the first place. Conservationists hope to see it growing again in its natural habitat and perhaps one day becoming a badge of honour for a new generation of environmentally conscious farmers.
